As the saying goes, “Everyone is entitled to their own opinion, but not their own facts.” It is particularly important to understand that point when an ostensibly “objective” news site like Newsweek.com prints blatant lies about the marijuana reform movement.

Their most recent contribution is America’s Marijuana Legalization Experiment Is Going Up in Smoke (Mar. 12, 2024). It is a tour de force of prohibitionist propaganda. This article is typical of what Newsweek has been printing for the last several years.

This isn’t just biased reporting — it’s a part of a campaign of singularly dishonest journalism from the editorial level.

Ironically, Newsweek claims to have journalistic standards: POLICIES AND STANDARDS – NEWSWEEK MISSION STATEMENT

The Setup: “When marijuana legalization first started gaining momentum in the United States, it was heralded as a progressive step toward criminal justice reform, economic growth and public health benefits. Advocates promised that legal cannabis would eliminate the illicit market, generate tax revenue and ensure a safe, well-regulated industry. That is not how things have turned out.”

First, “marijuana legalization” in general terms really has been “a progressive step toward criminal justice reform, economic growth and public health benefits.”

In fact, taking a significant part of the huge retail and wholesale marijuana market out of the black market has been a major step “toward criminal justice reform, economic growth and public health benefits.”

And marijuana arrests (no mention of them here) are down from a peak of 870,000 in 2007 (over 85% for simple possession) to “only” 227,108. Of that number, 92% were for possession only.

See: Weed Arrests Were Nearly A Quarter Million Last Year, Per FBI Data

“Federal law enforcement officials in 2024 — the last for which data is available — charged fewer than 500 people with marijuana trafficking, according to data provided by the US Sentencing Commission.”

The total marks a 93 percent decline in federal marijuana trafficking arrests since 2012, when Colorado and Washington became the first two states to regulate the adult-use marijuana market. Annual data provided by the Sentencing Commission’s Sourcebook on Federal Sentencing Statistics shows that marijuana trafficking arrests have fallen every year since then.

Maybe Newsweek thinks that not arresting millions of Americans is a cost, not a benefit.

As for “economic growth,” it is harder to measure because it is impossible to know how big the drop in illegal sales has been. On the other hand, states do keep track of sales taxes — and it has provided multi-billions in revenue. Seriously.

See:Marijuana Tax Revenue by State These 23 States, DC Collected $2.9 Billion in Cannabis Excise Tax Revenue in 2023

Nonetheless, no one in the cannabis industry can be happy with the muddled mess of continuing federal prohibition that makes it very difficult for cannabis retailers to take credit cards and have regular bank accounts.

Consequently, the industry is compelled to have lots of cash on hand, which makes them targets for armed robberies. Then the prohibitionists at Newsweek blame the regulated marijuana industry, not the prohibition-related restrictions that make the industry a target.

However, moving a huge, well-established black market into a regulated industry was never going to be easy politically. A significant number of cannabis consumers were happy with their suppliers, and a lot of artisanal growers were making a living “gardening” — and there is no point in putting them out of business.

Then politicians get involved. Newsweek reveals, surprise, surprise: “In New York, legalization has turned into what even the progressive Governor Kathy Hochul has called ‘a disaster.’”

Well, let’s look at what the libertarian Reason magazine says: New York’s Weed Nightmare – Reason

“Taxes on legal weed are exorbitantly high, leading most consumers to continue buying from the illegal market. One cannabis industry lobbyist estimated toward the end of 2023 that as much as 90 percent of New Yorkers still purchase weed illegally — two and a half years after legalization.”

Was that the fault of the marijuana industry? While the city wanted to limit the number of licensed marijuana retailers to 190, it is worth noting that there are over 13,000 bodegas in New York City that sell beer and tobacco, including tobacco leaves that are used to make “blunts,” a form of marijuana cigarette.

Amsterdam, with a population of 930,000, has roughly 160 licensed marijuana “coffee shops,” while New York City has over 8 million people — so it would seem that it should have at least 1,500 licensed cannabis stores.

Amsterdam gets approximately 8 million visitors per year:Tourism in Amsterdam – Statista

New York City got 64 million visitors in 2024, the New York Post reported:NYC drew 64M visitors in 2024 – New York Post

That is eight times as many as Amsterdam. So by that measure, what used to be called New Amsterdam should have approximately 1,200 licensed cannabis stores.

(By the way, cannabis has been sold over the counter in The Netherlands, not just Amsterdam, for almost fifty years, and the rate of Dutch cannabis use is approximately half that of the United States.)

See: Cannabis use by country – Wikipedia

Meanwhile, the “land of the free” has arrested approximately twice the current population of The Netherlands during that time for simple possession of cannabis. No mention in Newsweek.

And now for a non sequitur: “Critics argue that the public was misled about the risks of high-potency pot that has flooded the legal market.”

It “flooded the legal market,” but we were just told that the problem is that most of the business stayed in the illegal market — especially in New York.???

And the dangers of “potent pot” in the contraband market have been a part of the prohibitionist party line for decades.

See: The Perils of Potent Pot Party Line – MarijuanaNews.com

The real difference is that buyers in the legal market can at least know what they are buying. Although the labels tend to overstate the THC levels.

Then we are told: “A growing number of experts, politicians and even former supporters of legalization are questioning whether states that rolled out legal weed got it wrong.”

And who is the “expert” he cites? Why it is: “Keith Humphreys, a professor at Stanford University specializing in drug policy, argues that legalization was sold to the public on overly optimistic premises.”

Keith Humphreys – Wikipedia has a doctorate in psychology — this is an example of appealing to an authority outside his area of expertise. E.g., Einstein was a socialist, so socialism must be better than capitalism.

Supporting marijuana prohibition may be his hobby or hobby horse, but it is not his area of expertise that connects him with Stanford, an otherwise great university.

Do a Google search for “Keith Humphreys marijuana” and then take the day off to read the results. It is my expert opinion as an economist that he suffers from an obsession with marijuana and should consult with a psychologist in hopes of finding a cure. Maybe some CBD.

Humphreys says: “We regulate the alcohol industry by limiting proof levels — no one can legally sell 190-proof liquor in a bar. We should do the same with marijuana.”

Well, liquor stores that sell alcohol for off-premises consumption actually do sell 190-proof alcohol, which would be fatal in relatively small amounts — but it’s clearly labeled, unlike moonshine.

And the bars that sensibly will not sell you 190-proof, will happily sell you shots of 95 proof whatever. (I am a self-trained expert on this subject, but I did do research at Yale.)

So, should we regulate cannabis like alcohol, and let consumers know the level of active ingredient — and let it be decided by the consumer?

Newsweek says: “Beyond market failures, critics argue that the increased potency of today’s marijuana — often exceeding 20 percent THC, compared with the 3–5 percent THC typical in pot grown and sold (illegally) in the 1990s — is contributing to a rise in cannabis-related health issues, especially among teenagers who do not yet have fully developed cognitive function.” (Emphasis added)

Teenagers can buy from the contraband market, but not the legal market, which has a minimum age of twenty-one. And most teenagers don’t know about — and can’t afford — the premium products.

But Humphreys claims: “We have moved from an era where the typical marijuana user consumed a low-potency product once a week to a market where the typical user consumes high-potency products daily… That’s about a 65-fold increase in exposure each week for the average cannabis user, and we don’t know the full effects of that.”

A 65-fold increase? For the average cannabis user? Citation, please!

There is zero evidence that there has been any such thing. I am happy to report that the quality of cannabis has improved over the last 58 years that I have been enjoying it. The problem with estimating average THC levels of contraband is simply “sampling.”

How representative of the total was the contraband seized and tested?

And marijuana users have been coping with the difference in THC levels for decades. Small joints are called “pinners” and larger joints are called “fatties.” Also, the difference between 5% THC and 15% THC is two puffs. Higher mathematics?

And who is the other authority cited by Newsweek? Now here is where Newsweek gets really sleazy. They introduce this one simply as: “Kevin Sabet, president of nonprofit Smart Approaches to Marijuana, has been an outspoken critic of the current commercialization model.”

In fact, Sabet is a regular contributor to Newsweek. Here is the link to his articles: Kevin Sabet – Newsweek Author Page

As I have said many times before, the way to tell the difference between prohibitionist and anti-prohibitionist websites is simple: we have links to their websites, but they almost never link to ours. We want you to see their lies. Freedom has nothing to fear from the truth.

And as the Baháʼí Faith teaches: “Truthfulness is the foundation of all the virtues of the world of humanity. Without truthfulness, progress and success in all of the worlds of God are impossible for a soul.”

So who is Sabet? Kevin Sabet – Wikipedia: “He is a former three-time White House Office of National Drug Control Policy advisor, having been the only person appointed to that office by both a Republican (George W. Bush) and Democrat (Obama and Clinton administrations).”

Sabet is a professional prohibitionist who brags about working for the Drug Czar’s office when it opposed any changes in the cannabis laws — including decriminalizing simple possession or even arresting medical marijuana patients.

See: I’m A Doctor and I Went to College with Kevin Sabet; He’s Still Up To No Good

While Newsweek only says that Sabet works for a nonprofit, consider how Newsweek introduces the opposition: “Cat Packer, director of drug markets and legal regulation at the Drug Policy Alliance, a pro-legalization special interest group.” (Emphasis added)

Ooh, “pro-legalization special interest group.” Evil incorporated.

(Disclosure: I was a founding Board Member of the Drug Policy Foundation, one of the predecessors of the DPA; I am pro-legalization; I am a former National Director of NORML.org; and I am the President of Weed.de, a German cannabis company — and I am not trying to hide it from anyone.)

Sabet claims: “Today’s marijuana is strengthened by very high-potency growing methods that have resulted in record levels of psychosis, schizophrenia, suicide, IQ loss and other issues..”Citation, please!

On Psychosis: State Cannabis Legalization and Psychosis-Related Health Care Utilization

“The findings of this study do not support an association between state policies legalizing cannabis and psychosis-related outcomes.” (Professor Humphreys was one of the authors.)

On IQ Loss: Association of Cannabis With Cognitive Functioning in Adolescents and Young Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis

“Associations between cannabis use and cognitive functioning in cross-sectional studies of adolescents and young adults are small and may be of questionable clinical importance for most individuals. Furthermore, abstinence of longer than 72 hours diminishes cognitive deficits associated with cannabis use.”

On Suicide: Suicidality Risk After Using Cannabis and Cannabinoids: An Umbrella Review

“There is an association between cannabis use and suicide in adolescents, but which is cause or effect? Are they suicidal because they use cannabis, or do they use cannabis because they are suicidal? Correlation is not causation.”

Consider: “On the contrary, current evidence indicates that therapeutic cannabis is safe. In conclusion, the literature supports the cannabis-suicidality association in recreational use but considers cannabidiol safe for treatment. Further studies with quantitative and interventional approaches are recommended.”

Also consider: The United States ranks 31st for suicides, while The Netherlands — where cannabis has been sold over-the-counter for almost fifty years — ranks 84th. List of countries by suicide rate – Wikipedia

Teen Suicide Rates: Association Between Marijuana Laws and Suicide Among 12- to 25-Year-Olds in the United States From 2000 to 2019

“MML and RML were associated with increased suicide-related mortality in female youth and 14-to-16-year-olds of both sexes…”

Of course, teenagers cannot legally buy cannabis, so why should there be any causal correlation?

In the near future I will be dealing more with the dire public health claims made by prohibitionists in otherwise respectable publications, but my point in this article is simply that Newsweek does not adhere to the journalistic standards that it proclaims.

In other words, “bad journalism” is still the best two-word explanation for marijuana prohibition, and Newsweek is a regular outlet for prohibitionist propaganda.
